intro: Thérèse Dussaut plays the piano original of Ravel’s Pavane, a stately dance imagined for a princess at the old Spanish court. The melody returns several times, each time with more movement beneath its long notes.

sections.label: A · Refrain in G major
sections.mNote: Long melody notes over even quavers.

sections.label: B · Chords over held low B
sections.mNote: Très lointain; a chordal melody over held bass octaves.

sections.label: A′ · Refrain over fuller chords
sections.mNote: The first tune returns over a heavier bass.

sections.label: C · Soft legato line after fortissimo
sections.mNote: Subitement très doux et très lié: suddenly soft and connected.

sections.label: A″ · Refrain over semiquaver accompaniment
sections.mNote: Ravel marks the melody to stand out above the semiquavers.

relations.label: The refrain returns
relations.basis: The first return of A follows the contrasting B episode in the work’s A–B–A–C–A design; the later excerpt lies inside the refrain marked near 114 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.925, sustained 25.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 110.5 s (cache/form/ravel-pavane.txt, candidate 4; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The refrain returns for the close
relations.basis: After the broader C episode, the refrain returns again near 244 s. This pair compares the earlier refrain return with the final one, rather than claiming a new theme. CENS diagonal mean 0.954, sustained 27.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 132 s (cache/form/ravel-pavane.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening melody on G
cues.text: The melody holds its first note, G, while the accompaniment plays detached quavers beneath it. Ravel marked the passage “Assez doux, mais d’une sonorité large”.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, plate E. 623 D., p. 1: opening G, detached quavers and Assez doux, mais d’une sonorité large. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP384819-PMLP03577-Maurice_Ravel_-_Pavane_pour_une_infante_d%C3%A9funte.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Commission and dedication
cues.text: The Princesse de Polignac commissioned the piece and received its dedication. Fauré, Ravel’s teacher, had introduced him to her Paris salon. Ricardo Viñes gave the public première on 5 April 1902 at the Société nationale de musique.
cues.evidence: Bru Zane records the commission, dedication, Fauré’s introduction and Viñes’s première on 5 April 1902 at the Société nationale de musique. https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/pavane-infante-defunte-maurice-ravel

cues.title: Très lointain, over low B octaves
cues.text: Très lointain — very distant. Low B octaves are held beneath a melody in closely spaced chords. The walking bass of the opening has stopped, and the chords move together above the held notes.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, p. 2: Très lointain, pp, low B octaves and the B-minor chordal melody.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The title and the Spanish court
cues.text: Ravel described the piece as a pavane that a young princess might have danced at the Spanish court centuries earlier. He orchestrated it in 1909, ten years after the piano original.
cues.evidence: Ravel’s explanation of the title: Bru Zane, https://www.bruzanemediabase.com/en/exploration/works/pavane-infante-defunte-maurice-ravel . Orchestration in August 1909 (published 1910): Manuel Cornejo, Ravel chronology (2018), https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf

cues.title: Sudden soft legato passage
cues.text: A broad fortissimo chord is followed by a line marked subitement très doux et très lié. B♭ colours the melody, and short connecting notes fill its gaps. Later the piano plays forcefully again.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 3–4: Large, ff, followed by the sudden soft instruction, B♭ and flowing upper notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Last refrain, new accompaniment
cues.text: The melody returns above a new accompaniment in flowing semiquavers. Ravel marks it marquez le chant, so the tune stands clear of the moving notes. Its long phrases stay recognisable while the accompaniment grows busier around them.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, p. 5: 1er Mouvement, marquez le chant and the refrain’s new semiquaver accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chord
cues.text: The ending broadens greatly. The last G major chord is marked fortissimo and held under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Demets piano edition, p. 5, last system: En élargissant beaucoup, final ff G-major chord and fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Walking bass stops on low B
transitions.to: B · Chords over held low B
transitions.how: The refrain broadens, then the tempo is restored and the next phrase is marked Très lointain. Low B octaves hold beneath a B minor melody in chords. The piano’s walking bass stops, and the upper voices move together above it.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 1–2: broadening, restored tempo, Très lointain and B-minor chords over low B octaves.

transitions.title: Fermata before the G major return
transitions.from: B · Chords over held low B
transitions.how: Chromatic chords move to a close marked un peu plus lent, and a fermata holds the last chord. At Reprenez le mouvement the original tempo resumes and the G major refrain returns, now accompanied by fuller chords in the bass.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 2–3: chromatic closing chords, un peu plus lent, fermata and Reprenez le mouvement.

transitions.title: Fortissimo chord to a soft, legato line
transitions.to: C · Soft legato line after fortissimo
transitions.how: The G major refrain reaches a chord marked Large and fortissimo. A line marked subitement très doux et très lié follows. B♭ enters the melody, and the bass leaves more space beneath the upper notes.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 3–4: Large, ff, then subitement très doux et très lié and the chromatically inflected melody.

transitions.title: A 2/4 bar before the refrain
transitions.from: C · Soft legato line after fortissimo
transitions.how: The piano descends through chromatic chords. Ravel writes Très grave, shortens the bar to 2/4 and puts a fermata on the last chord. The G major refrain then resumes in four beats, with its melody above a new semiquaver accompaniment.
transitions.evidence: Demets piano edition, pp. 4–5: descending chords, Très grave, 2/4 bar, fermata and final refrain.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
